analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal extreme-heat early-warning system and funds community cooling projects.
analysis.headline: Introduced in August 2025 with ten Senate sponsors, all Democrats or independents, and referred to the Commerce Committee; no committee vote or floor action has followed.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stand up a permanent federal system, housed at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, to coordinate heat-health warnings, research, and planning across agencies. It would fund a National Academies study of gaps in heat preparedness, and create a grant program for cool roofs, shade, cooling centers, building retrofits, and grid reliability, with at least 40% of grant money required to go to low-income communities and communities with environmental justice concerns. It authorizes roughly $200 million over five years and would restore federal heat tools that the bill's findings say have been discontinued or limited.
analysis.who_benefits: People most exposed to extreme heat, which the bill's findings call the leading cause of weather-related death in the U.S.: adults over 65, outdoor and indoor workers, pregnant people, young children, people with disabilities, incarcerated people, people experiencing homelessness, and residents of low-income neighborhoods and communities of color that have less tree cover and air conditioning. States, Tribes, local governments, nonprofits, and academic institutions would receive the grants.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers, seniors, and low-income urban communities

how_it_helps.text: Creates an interagency committee and a NOAA-based system to coordinate federal heat warnings, data, and planning, so communities get consistent, open heat-health information.

Establishes a community grant program for cooling centers, cool roofs and pavements, tree planting, building retrofits, high-efficiency air conditioning, and grid reliability projects, and requires at least 40% of the money to go to communities with environmental justice concerns or low-income communities.

Requires a National Academies study of gaps in heat response, including which schools, prisons, and public facilities lack air conditioning, the demographics of heat victims, and how far the discontinuation of federal tools like the CDC Heat and Health Tracker has set back risk education and data collection.
The bill directs support toward establishing workplace policies and practices to reduce heat illness risk among workers, and prioritizes historically disadvantaged communities when awarding grants.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through roughly $201.5 million in authorized appropriations to NOAA over fiscal years 2026 through 2030: $100 million for the coordination system and committee, $1.5 million for the National Academies study, and $100 million for community heat resilience grants.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, about $200M over five years

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes but does not appropriate money, so Congress would still have to fund it each year, and roughly $200 million spread over five years and dozens of agencies is small against the scale of a problem its own findings say causes more than 65,000 emergency room visits a year.

On worker heat protections, the strongest single intervention available, the bill only directs study and grant support for workplace policies; it does not create any enforceable federal heat standard for outdoor and indoor workers.
The bill leans heavily on interagency committees, strategic plans, and studies, which take years to produce and depend on agencies actually implementing them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost is modest and the problem it targets is the nation's leading weather-related killer, concentrated among people with the fewest resources to protect themselves. The honest weakness is design: no enforceable workplace heat standard, and much of the bill's machinery is planning and study rather than direct protection, so its real-world effect depends on the grant program being funded and used well.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in August 2025 and referred to the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee, where it has sat with no further action since.

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced the bill on August 1, 2025, with nine cosponsors: eight Senate Democrats and one independent, Senator Sanders; no Republican has joined.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day; the full action history shows no markup, vote, or floor action since.

The bill's findings state that extreme heat has been the leading cause of weather-related death in the United States over the last 30 years, and that several federal heat tools, including the CDC Heat and Health Tracker and the National Weather Service HeatRisk portal, have been discontinued, dismantled, or limited in public accessibility.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost; the bill is waiting in committee, and the communities most exposed to extreme heat continue without the coordination or funding it would provide.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet; the bill sits in committee

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled ten initial Senate sponsors.

for.name: 9 Senate cosponsors
for.role: 8 of 45 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate independents, including Sen. Padilla, Sen. Booker, and Sen. Sanders

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors are Democrats or independents and no Republican has cosponsored, but no one has opposed it on the record and no vote has occurred.

industries.note: Grant-funded cool roofs, pavement, tree planting, and air conditioning retrofits would create work for these industries while delivering cooling to residents; their interest here runs alongside the public's.

The bill funds grid-resilience projects to keep air conditioning running during heat waves, but also supports protections against energy shutoffs and consumer rebate assistance, which cut against utilities' interest in disconnecting nonpaying customers.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to the Senate Commerce Committee that sit for months without a markup, and that draw no cosponsors from the majority party, rarely reach the floor on their own; the likeliest paths are that it dies at the end of the 119th Congress or that its ideas get attached to a larger weather or disaster bill if its sponsors can win Republican support.
